comments.story: Ask HN: What cool skill or project interests you, but feels out of reach?
comments.text: For me, it's Bézier curves --- Freya Holmér has a wonderful video on them: [VIDEO] and I've been trying to read through _METAFONT: The Program_ and [LINK] and I keep wondering if I shouldn't just try scripting Inkscape.... I want to do a couple of different things, and not sure if they all fit in one project or no: - implement a single line font in my current project: [LINK] - implement a way to convert arbitrary curves into smooth arcs (for DXFs or G2/G3 arcs for G-code) - work up an interactive version of METAFONT/METAPOST which allows both programming and drawing

Another upvote for Freya Holmér's amazing video "The Continuity of Splines". She covers the insightful "reflection test" around the 28:05 mark: [VIDEO] and actual "curvature combs" at 32:26. Finally, she covers the continuity of curvature combs that B-Splines exhibit around the 54:00 mark: [VIDEO]

comments.text: I didn't really understand Bézier splines until I watched this excellent video [0] from Freya Holmér. It talks about various kinds of splines, and the various equations behind them. If this paper is interesting to you, you may also be interested in this amazingly well done video on the continuation of splines. It isn't exactly the same thing, and delves into some deeper concepts, but I've watched it like 3 times over the last year. [VIDEO]

comments.story: Bezier-rs – algorithms for Bézier segments and shapes
comments.text: Anytime béziers are mentioned on HN, I feel compelled to share these absolutely incredible videos from Freya Holmér [VIDEO] (73 minutes) [LINK] (24 minutes)
If splines/beziers are of any interest to you, I could not recommend these videos from Freya Holmer enough. [VIDEO] [LINK]
the splines yt video ( [VIDEO] ) is (IMHO) one of the best educational videos on a programming topic, full stop.

A wonderful example of this is: The Continuity of Splines [VIDEO] and The Beauty of Bézier Curves [LINK] by Freya Holmér [LINK] While not animated, I find: _Euclid's Elements_ (Joyce's Java Version) very helpful [LINK] Since my current project has pretty much devolved to putting a UI on various trigonometric functions and allowing the user to program them, I'd be very glad of other resources in this space (currently working through Hilbert's _Geometry and the Imagination_ and the book which matches [LINK] and just finished the _Make:Geometry/Trigonometry/Calculus_ series, and have had recommended Curves and Surfaces for CAGD: A Practical Guide by Gerald Farin)

I've been reading through a PDF on my Kindle Scribe which I downloaded from the original site --- it's a great overview, and most importantly, includes citations and references to the various papers where folks shared their research/progress. These days of course, one would just get _The Essentials of CAGD_ and similar texts, or read: [LINK] or watch: [VIDEO] Highly recommended for anyone who wants an understanding of how modern CAD software came about. For my part, I have found it invaluable in working on my current project as described at: [LINK]

comments.story: A 37-year-old wanting to learn computer science
comments.text: I've been re-learning CS (programmed as a kid, then missed getting a minor in CS in college after the service by one 300-level course which wasn't being re-offered when I needed it) and then just did (La)TeX and AppleScript for my day job, but am now trying to create a tool for CNC which is quite different from those which have existed previously, and one thing which has helped a lot is MIT OCW: - the Python courses got me up-to-speed on the basics of that language: [LINK] and [LINK] - Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs served as a disciplined review of a book which I wasn't patient enough to do the exercises of when I first read it: [LINK] - Mathematics for Computer Science helped make up for my spotty math: [LINK] I've also found the recent book: [LINK] very helpful (first reading I did one chapter at a time, re-writing my current project applying the principles of that…

Freya Holmer, of The Continuity of Splines [0] fame, recently gave a great conference talk about how quaternions naturally arise from the desire to define the multiplication of two vectors if you just agree to one new axiom : v^2 = ||v||^2, or "the square of a vector is equal to the square of its norm". It was fascinating and entertaining and I highly recommend anyone who finds this stuff interesting but confusing (like I do) to check it out: [LINK] [0] [VIDEO]

comments.text: Short chrome browser extension I wrote some time ago that rewrites normal urls to videos like this: [VIDEO] into embedded video urls like this [VIDEO] bypassing ads and running video in full browser window.
